A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work and contain readable main text, equations, figures, references, and appendices. All 30 pages of each version support comparison, including the reorganized proofs.

before.justification: v1 reports original GPT-2 experiments on PKU-SafeRLHF in Figures 2–4 and numerical simulations supporting propositions in Figure 5.

after.justification: v2 retains the original language-model experiments in Figures 2–4 and numerical simulations in Figure 5.

M1.justification: The RLHF, DPO, online DPO/PILAF procedures, token-level model parameterizations, and retained relative ℓ1 estimator remain unchanged. Section 5 renames the pairwise training loss a regression surrogate and corrects its malformed reward-difference notation without establishing a different implemented procedure. The revised constructions concern theoretical analysis.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same PKU-SafeRLHF QA, prompt, safer, and better data, the same model-misspecification scenarios, and the same three-action numerical simulations. The revised DTSP proof does not introduce an additional evaluated task.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is unchanged: Figures 2–3 compare online DPO with RL/RLHF, Figure 4 compares offline DPO with reward modeling, and Figure 5 retains the same gradient comparisons in each panel. Newly cited theoretical work is not evaluated as a baseline.

E3.justification: Section 5 and the implementation appendices retain the same GPT-2 models, data splits, sample counts, freezing controls, metrics, reward scales, and training budgets. The numerical simulations also retain their reward vectors, regularization parameter, and parameter range.

E4.justification: The reward-scale analysis at 0.4, 1, and 4, model-misspecification comparisons, sample-size analysis from 1k to 9k examples, and numerical counterexamples are retained. Revised captions explain existing analyses rather than adding new tests.

E5.justification: Both versions state that experiments use three seeds and retain identical plotted uncertainty information. No repeated-run counts, statistical tests, or uncertainty-reporting practices are added or revised.

E6.justification: Figures 2–5 retain identical embedded plot content, including curves, rankings, and uncertainty displays. The appendix also retains the numerical comparison of approximately 0.729 for RLHF versus 2/3 for DPO. No experimental result entries or findings are added or removed.

T1.justification: The finite-sample argument is substantially revised. v1's separate ℓ0 sparse-recovery guarantee and construction are removed; the retained separation becomes v2's informal Theorem 10 and formal Theorem 13 under explicit Assumptions 11–12. Lemma 1 changes its sample requirement from the trace of the Gram matrix to the trace of its inverse, and v2 adds an O(d) inverse-trace assumption. The separation proof replaces the tailored reference policy with one independent of the first token. Appendix B.11 also corrects the initial-token normalization using β log Z. Earlier performance-gap derivations remain elsewhere in the appendix.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central claims: relative RLHF/DPO performance depends on misspecification, online DPO can outperform both under isomorphism, and sparse rewards can create a finite-sample advantage for reward learning. The introductory rate notation is aligned with bounds already stated in v1.

C2.justification: Section 4 newly connects the finite-sample argument to asymptotic on-policy optimization and explicitly qualifies DTSP as a specific construction. Figure 2's caption now attributes the reward-scale trend to the second-order deviation in the online DPO objective. The limitations concerning small models and the absence of a practical BT-model alternative remain.

D1.justification: v1's Appendix D promises a future code release; v2's Appendix C states that code is released and supplies a project repository address. Section 5 also clarifies the pairwise-regression loss notation. Dataset, model, hyperparameter, hardware, and runtime disclosures otherwise match.

R1.justification: v2 adds Candes, Romberg, and Tao (2006) and explicitly connects the sparse-recovery ingredients to classical compressed sensing in Appendix B.10.1. Remark 3 additionally positions the persistent gap with PILAF as an overlooked nuance. The broader RLHF/DPO literature survey is moved from the appendix, not newly added.

P1.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes the theoretical narrative: token-level q-function discussion moves into Section 3.3, Section 4 is rewritten around reward-estimation error, and general related work moves into Section 6. The appendix separates preliminary lemmas, formal assumptions, theorem statements, and proofs, while consolidating other calculations. These changes extend beyond renumbering.

P2.justification: All five figures are retained. Figure 1 adopts prompt-conditioned notation, Figures 2–3 receive revised explanatory captions, and the plots occupy a more compact arrangement on page 9. Appendix material is repaginated, but the overall visual format and result displays remain substantially the same.

improvement.justification: v2 offers limited gains in clarity and reproducibility through explicit finite-sample assumptions, a corrected token-normalization derivation in Appendix B.11, clearer organization, and a stated code release with access information. Removing the separate ℓ0 result narrows theoretical coverage, while the empirical evidence and central conclusions remain unchanged. The gains make the argument easier to inspect without establishing a substantial overall advance.
